title: Dynamic programming
summary: Reuse answers to overlapping subproblems after defining a clear state.

parts.rule: Use dynamic programming when optimal substructure meets overlapping subproblems. Name a state that captures what still matters, write how states depend on earlier states, then fill bottom-up or memoize top-down. The complexity is roughly (number of states) times (work per transition). If you cannot name the state, you are not ready to allocate the table.
parts.why: Bare recursion revisits the same subproblem exponentially often. DP pays for each state once. Weak answers draw a table with no spoken state meaning, or jump to DP when a greedy proof already suffices. Strong answers lead with state, transition, and fill order before touching code.
parts.example: Ways to climb n=4 stairs using steps of 1 or 2: let dp[i] be the number of ways to reach i. Set dp[0]=1, dp[1]=1, and dp[i]=dp[i-1]+dp[i-2]. Then dp[2]=2, dp[3]=3, dp[4]=5, each index filled once. Fewest coins from [1, 3, 4] to make 6: dp[x] = fewest coins for sum x, dp[0]=0, others start at a large sentinel. Relax every coin across increasing x until dp[6]=2 via 3+3, which beats greedy 4+1+1. States equal target+1; each tries three coins. On a 2x3 grid counting paths only right or down, dp[r][c] = dp[r-1][c] + dp[r][c-1] with the first row and column seeded as 1 — six cells, each constant work.
parts.use: Reach for DP on knapsack-style budgets, grid path counts, edit distance, longest increasing subsequence variants, and any recurrence you would otherwise recompute. Prefer memoization when few states are reachable; prefer tabulation when every state is needed inside tight loops.

body:
Rule. Use dynamic programming when optimal substructure meets overlapping subproblems. Name a state that captures what still matters, write how states depend on earlier states, then fill bottom-up or memoize top-down. The complexity is roughly (number of states) times (work per transition). If you cannot name the state, you are not ready to allocate the table.

Why it matters. Bare recursion revisits the same subproblem exponentially often. DP pays for each state once. Weak answers draw a table with no spoken state meaning, or jump to DP when a greedy proof already suffices. Strong answers lead with state, transition, and fill order before touching code.

Worked example. Ways to climb n=4 stairs using steps of 1 or 2: let dp[i] be the number of ways to reach i. Set dp[0]=1, dp[1]=1, and dp[i]=dp[i-1]+dp[i-2]. Then dp[2]=2, dp[3]=3, dp[4]=5, each index filled once. Fewest coins from [1, 3, 4] to make 6: dp[x] = fewest coins for sum x, dp[0]=0, others start at a large sentinel. Relax every coin across increasing x until dp[6]=2 via 3+3, which beats greedy 4+1+1. States equal target+1; each tries three coins. On a 2x3 grid counting paths only right or down, dp[r][c] = dp[r-1][c] + dp[r][c-1] with the first row and column seeded as 1 — six cells, each constant work.

When to use. Reach for DP on knapsack-style budgets, grid path counts, edit distance, longest increasing subsequence variants, and any recurrence you would otherwise recompute. Prefer memoization when few states are reachable; prefer tabulation when every state is needed inside tight loops.

When to refuse. Skip DP when subproblems do not overlap — plain recursion or a DAG walk may be enough. Skip a table that you cannot define in words. Skip DP when a proven greedy structure is simpler. Skip exponential state spaces labeled as DP without compression or meet-in-the-middle ideas.
